description: We’re building a 3D Lunar Landing Site Navigator that shows where and when south-pole landers get sunlight for power and Earth in view for comms. Our prototype already runs on real NASA LOLA terrain, with Sun and Earth positions checked against JPL Horizons. We love space, web 3D and data. Looking for: planetary science/engineering, three.js/front-end devs, UI/UX designers, and storytellers for our demo video. No Moon experience needed, just curiosity!
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a browser tool for choosing where and when to land near the Moon's south pole. It lights real NASA LRO LOLA terrain with the true Sun and Earth, traces the horizon around each candidate site, and shows when the site is sunlit (power) and when Earth is in view (direct-to-Earth communication). Mission planners, students and the public can compare sites side by side, find the best landing date for a given mission length, and see how moving a few hundred metres changes the outcome. The Sun and Earth positions match NASA/JPL Horizons to within 0.005°. It runs in any browser, with no install, and the first view appears in about a second.
details:
The problem

The lunar south pole is where Artemis and many robotic missions want to land, because it has water ice and long sunlit ridges. Near the pole the Sun skims the horizon and the Earth sits low. A crater rim a few kilometres away can cut a lander's solar power or its link to Earth for days. Two sites 400 m apart can differ by tens of percentage points in sunlight. Answering "where and when should we land?" means tracing the real terrain against the real Sun and Earth, hour by hour.

What it does

The screen has three linked parts that share one time and one selected site:

  • The Moon: 3D terrain of everything south of 80°S, on the true curved Moon, lit by the real Sun with cast shadows. A sky view below it shows the full horizon around the site with the Sun's and Earth's paths.
  • The site: countdowns to the next sunset, sunrise, Earthset and Earthrise, the Sun and Earth elevation, and window statistics.
  • The deck: every site as a row on one time axis, with sunlight, Earth in view, both together, the longest night and the longest communication gap. The best value in each column is highlighted.

Users can:

  1. Compare candidate sites, add them from a library (Artemis candidate regions, IM-1, IM-2, LCROSS, Apollo 11, 15 and 17, Blue Ghost, Chandrayaan-3, Chang'e 4 and 6), type coordinates anywhere on the Moon, or click the terrain.
  2. Pick a mission length and see the best landing date for each site, or a "landing score" map of every possible landing time.
  3. Run a nearby scan of a 5 × 5 grid of points 400 m apart, to see how much a small move changes the result.
  4. Set an exact UTC time, play time forward, copy a link that reopens the same scenario, and export a site's time series as CSV.

How it works

  • Terrain: the LOLA polar elevation model, averaged to 160 m per pixel, a 3800 × 3800 grid of 14.4 million heights.
  • Horizons: for each site the tool casts 1,440 rays across the terrain on the curved Moon and records the highest elevation angle every 0.5° of azimuth.
  • Sun and Earth: positions from Astronomy Engine, rotated into the Moon-fixed frame with the IAU lunar rotation model, with topocentric parallax.
  • Sunlight is the fraction of the solar disc above the horizon. Earth in view is Earth's centre above the horizon plus a user-set margin.
  • Landing dates: each possible landing time is scored by averaging sunlight, Earth in view, and both together over the mission.

To make 14.4 million heights fast to load, we wrote a lossless codec (a terrain predictor plus a four-stream rANS entropy coder in eight bands). It cuts the data to 7.3 MB, 30% smaller than gzip. Helper threads decode the bands in parallel in 75 ms. A 0.8 MB preview draws first, so the Moon appears in under half a second on a fast connection, and the app is ready in about one second.

Validation

  • Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation match NASA/JPL Horizons (DE441) in 2,800 comparisons at four polar sites over 2026–2027. The worst error is 0.005°, about 1/120 of the Sun's diameter.
  • Shackleton crater's floor gets 0% sunlight and never sees Earth, as expected for a permanently shadowed region.
  • The tool's best-lit point on the Shackleton–de Gerlache ridge (89.44°S, 222.63°E, about 89% sunlight in 2027) lands next to the "connecting ridge" point cited in the literature.
  • Apollo 11 gets a 14.8-day night with Earth always 58° to 73° up. Chang'e 4 on the far side never sees Earth.
  • A test script checks the landing-date maths against brute force on the real terrain.

Benefits and impact

  • Planners and students get a site-selection study that usually takes specialist software, in a browser tab, in seconds.
  • Decisions are visible: a shared link reopens the exact site, date and mission, so a team can argue over the same picture.
  • The public can see why the south pole is hard and why Artemis landing regions sit on ridges and massifs.

What's creative

  • One shared clock: the 3D Moon, the sky view and every site's timeline move together, so dragging time shows shadows, sunsets and Earthsets at once.
  • A landing-date planner, not just a map: the tool answers "when" as well as "where", with a score for every possible landing hour.
  • Our own terrain codec: we packed 14.4 million NASA heights losslessly into 7.3 MB and decode them on several threads, so real terrain runs in a browser tab.

Factors we considered

  • Power: sunlight is the share of the solar disc above the real horizon, not just the Sun's centre.
  • Communication: Earth in view is checked with a user-set margin above the horizon, and the longest blackout is reported.
  • Mission length: results are averaged over the mission, because a site that is good on landing day can go dark a week later.
  • Nearby ground: the nearby scan shows how sensitive a site is to landing errors of a few hundred metres.
  • Trust: every number is checked against NASA/JPL Horizons and brute-force tests.

Limits

Terrain is 160 m per pixel, so boulders and small craters are not modelled. There is no terrain north of 80°S, so sites off the map use a smooth horizon. Earth in view is line of sight, not a radio link budget. The tool is for study and education, not flight operations.

Built with

JavaScript, three.js, Astronomy Engine, Web Workers, Python (NumPy) for data preparation, and Node.js for validation, tests and the speed benchmark. It is a static site with no build step.
dataRefs: LRO LOLA South Polar Elevation Model LDEM_80S_80M (NASA PDS)
NASA/JPL Horizons System (DE441 ephemeris, used for validation)
